title: III. An Onion
paragraphs: Grushenka lived in the busiest part of town, close to the cathedral square. Her home was a small wooden lodge in the courtyard of the widow Morozov’s house, a big, old, very ugly stone building of two stories. The widow lived quietly with her two nieces, both unmarried and both getting on in years. She had no need to take a lodger. Yet everyone knew she had taken Grushenka in four years earlier for one reason only, to oblige her kinsman, the merchant Samsonov, who was known to be the girl’s protector. People said the jealous old man had parked his “favorite” with the widow Morozov so that the old woman would watch the new lodger’s conduct closely. That close watching soon turned out to be pointless. In the end the widow seldom saw Grushenka and never troubled her with supervision of any kind. True, it was four years since the old man had fetched her from the chief town of the province, a girl of eighteen, slim, delicate, shy, timid, dreamy and sad, and a good deal had happened since then. Little was known in town about her past, and what was known was vague. Nothing more had come out in the four years, even though many people had grown interested in the beautiful young woman that Agrafena Alexandrovna had turned into. Rumor had it that at seventeen she had been betrayed by someone, some officer, and dropped by him at once. The officer had gone off and later married, and Grushenka was left in poverty and disgrace. Yet it was also said that, although old Samsonov had pulled her out of destitution, she came of a respectable family from the clergy, and was the daughter of a deacon or some such person.

Now, four years later, the sensitive, wounded, pitiful little orphan had grown into a plump, rosy beauty of the true Russian kind, bold and strong-minded, proud and insolent. She had a head for business, was greedy for gain, thrifty and shrewd, and by fair means or foul had managed, so it was said, to build up a small fortune. On one point alone there was agreement. Grushenka was hard to get near. Apart from her aged protector, not a single man in those four years could boast of her favors. That was a plain fact, because plenty of men, especially in the last two years, had tried to win them. It had all been wasted effort. A few of these suitors had had to retreat in an undignified, even comical way, beaten by the firm and ironical resistance of this strong-willed young woman. People knew, too, that lately she had taken to what is called “speculation” and had shown a real talent for it. So many were saying she was no better than a Jew. She did not lend money at interest. But it was known, for example, that for some time she had been buying up bad debts for next to nothing, a tenth of their face value, in partnership with old Karamazov, and had then made ten times that value out of them.

The old widower Samsonov was a very rich man, and stingy and merciless. He bullied his grown sons. But in the last year, since falling ill and losing the use of his swollen legs, he had come greatly under the sway of his protégée. At first he had kept her strictly and in humble circumstances, “on Lenten fare,” as the wits of the time put it. But Grushenka had contrived to free herself, and at the same time she had planted in him an unlimited belief in her fidelity. The old man, long dead now, had once run a large business and was a remarkable character too, miserly and hard as flint. Her hold on him was so strong that he could not live without her (especially in the last two years). Even so, he settled no real fortune on her, and he would not have done it even if she had threatened to leave him. He did give her a small sum, though, and everyone was amazed when that came out.

“You’re a girl with brains,” he told her when he handed over eight thousand roubles, “so look out for yourself. But I’ll tell you this: besides your yearly allowance, which you get as before, you’ll have nothing more from me until the day I die, and I’ll leave you nothing in my will either.”

And he kept his word. He died and left everything to his sons, men he had treated as servants all his life, together with their wives and children. Grushenka was not even named in the will. All this was learned later. What he did give her was advice, on how to increase her capital, and he steered business her way.

Fyodor Pavlovitch first met Grushenka over a speculative deal, and to his own astonishment he ended up madly in love with her. Old Samsonov, sick as he was, found this enormously funny. It is worth noting that Grushenka was always completely and spontaneously frank with the old man. He seems to have been the one person in the world she was frank with. Lately, when Dmitri also entered the scene with his love, the old man stopped laughing. Instead, he once gave Grushenka some stern and serious advice.

“If you have to pick between them, father or son, pick the old man. Just make sure first that the old scoundrel will marry you and put some money in your name. But don’t go on with the captain. No good will come of that.”
Those were the actual words of the old rake, who could already feel that his death was near. He did in fact die five months afterwards.

I will mention in passing that many in our town knew about the grotesque, monstrous rivalry of the Karamazovs, father and son, over Grushenka. Yet hardly anyone understood what lay behind her attitude to the two of them. Even her two servants (after the catastrophe I will describe later) stated in court that she had received Dmitri Fyodorovitch only out of fear, because “he threatened to murder her.” These servants were an old cook, ailing and nearly deaf, who had come from Grushenka’s old home, and the cook’s granddaughter, a bright girl of twenty who worked as a maid. Grushenka lived very economically, and nothing around her was luxurious. The lodge had three rooms, furnished with mahogany pieces in the style of 1820, which belonged to her landlady.

By the time Rakitin and Alyosha went in it was quite dark, and yet no lamps had been lit. Grushenka lay in her drawing-room on the big, hard, clumsy sofa with its mahogany back, which was covered in worn, cracked leather. She had two white down pillows from her bed under her head and lay flat on her back, perfectly still, hands clasped behind her head. She was dressed as if she were expecting someone, in a black silk dress and a dainty lace fichu on her head that suited her well. A lace shawl lay over her shoulders, fastened with a heavy gold brooch. Someone was certainly expected. She lay there restless and tired, her face a little pale, her lips and eyes feverish, and her right foot kept tapping the arm of the sofa. The arrival of Rakitin and Alyosha set off a small commotion. From the hall they heard Grushenka jump up from the sofa and call out in a frightened voice, “Who’s there?” But the maid had met the visitors and answered her mistress at once.
“It’s not him, it’s nothing, just other visitors.”
“What’s going on?” muttered Rakitin, taking Alyosha into the drawing-room.

Grushenka stood by the sofa, still looking alarmed. A thick coil of dark brown hair had come loose from its lace covering and lay over her right shoulder. She did not notice, and did not tuck it back, until she had stared at the visitors and made out who they were.
“Oh, it’s you, Rakitin? You gave me such a fright. Who’s this you’ve brought? Who’s that with you? Good heavens, you’ve brought him!” she cried, recognizing Alyosha.
“Have someone bring candles!” said Rakitin, with the easy manner of a close friend who has the right to give orders in the house.

“Candles ... of course, candles.... Fenya, bring him a candle.... Well, you picked a fine moment to bring him!” she cried again, nodding at Alyosha. She turned to the mirror and began pinning up her hair with both hands, fast. She seemed put out.
“Haven’t I managed to please you?” asked Rakitin, almost offended on the spot.

“You scared me, Rakitin, that’s all.” Grushenka turned to Alyosha with a smile. “Don’t be afraid of me, my dear Alyosha. You can’t imagine how glad I am to see you, my unexpected guest. But you scared me, Rakitin. I thought it was Mitya bursting in. You see, I just tricked him. I made him promise to believe me, and I told him a lie. I said I was going to spend the evening with my old man, Kuzma Kuzmitch, and would be there late, counting his money. Every week I spend a whole evening with him, going through his accounts. We shut ourselves in, and he counts on the abacus while I sit and enter the figures in the book. I’m the only one he trusts. Mitya thinks I’m there, but I came back, and I’ve been sitting here locked in, waiting for news. How did Fenya come to let you in? Fenya, Fenya, run to the gate, open it and look about for the captain! Maybe he’s hiding and spying. I’m terribly afraid.”
“There’s nobody there, Agrafena Alexandrovna. I just looked out. I keep running to peek through the crack. I’m trembling with fear myself.”

“Are the shutters bolted, Fenya? And we have to close the curtains—that’s better!” She pulled the heavy curtains shut herself. “He’d burst in straight away if he saw a light. I’m afraid of your brother Mitya today, Alyosha.”
Grushenka was talking loudly, and for all her alarm she seemed very happy about something.
“Why are you so afraid of Mitya today?” asked Rakitin. “I’d have thought you weren’t shy of him. You wind him round your little finger.”

“I tell you, I’m waiting for news, priceless news, and so I don’t want Mitya at all. And I feel that he didn’t believe I’d stay at Kuzma Kuzmitch’s. He must be lying in ambush now, in the garden behind Fyodor Pavlovitch’s, watching for me. And if he’s there, he won’t come here, which is all the better! But I really did go to Kuzma Kuzmitch’s. Mitya took me there himself. I told him I’d stay till midnight, and I asked him to be sure to come at midnight and take me home. He left, and I sat ten minutes with Kuzma Kuzmitch and came back here. Ugh, I was scared. I ran, so as not to bump into him.”
“And why are you all dressed up? What a funny cap you’ve got on!”
“Aren’t you nosy, Rakitin! I tell you, I’m waiting for a message. If it comes, I’ll fly, I’ll gallop off, and you won’t see me again. That’s why I’m dressed up. To be ready.”
“And where are you flying to?”
“If you know too much, you’ll get old too soon.”
“Well, I never! You’re thrilled ... I’ve never seen you like this. You’re dressed up as if for a ball.” Rakitin looked her over from head to foot.
“Much you know about balls.”
“And you know a lot about them?”

“I’ve seen a ball. The year before last, Kuzma Kuzmitch’s son got married, and I watched from the gallery. Do you think I want to chat with you, Rakitin, with a prince like this standing here? What a guest! Alyosha, my dear boy, I look at you and can’t believe my eyes. Good heavens, did you really come to see me? To tell the truth, it never entered my head that I’d see you. I never thought you’d come to me. It’s not the right moment, but I’m awfully glad to see you all the same. Sit down on the sofa, here, there, my bright young moon. I still can’t take it in.... Ah, Rakitin, if only you’d brought him yesterday or the day before! But I’m glad as it is! Maybe it’s better that he came now, at a moment like this, and not the day before yesterday.”

She sat down on the sofa next to Alyosha, in high spirits, and looked at him with plain delight. And she truly was glad. She was not lying when she said so. Her eyes shone and her lips laughed, but it was a kindly, merry laugh. Alyosha had not expected such a kind look on her face.... Before yesterday he had hardly met her. He had formed a frightening idea of her, and yesterday he had been horribly upset by the spiteful, treacherous trick she had played on Katerina Ivanovna. Now he was greatly surprised to find her quite different from what he had expected. Crushed as he was by his own grief, he found his eyes resting on her with attention, almost without meaning to. Her whole manner seemed changed for the better since yesterday. In her speech there was hardly a trace of that sugary sweetness, and in her movements none of that sensuous softness. Everything about her was simple and good-natured. Her gestures were quick, direct and trusting. But she was very excited.
“Goodness, how everything comes together today!” she chattered on. “And why I’m so glad to see you, Alyosha, I couldn’t tell you myself! Ask me, and I couldn’t say.”
“Oh, come on, you don’t know why you’re glad?” said Rakitin, grinning. “You were always badgering me to bring him. You had some aim in mind, I suppose.”

“I had a different aim once, but that’s over, and this isn’t the time. Listen, I want you to have something nice. I’m in such a good mood. You sit down too, Rakitin. Why are you standing? You’ve sat down already? Rakitin never forgets to look after himself. Look, Alyosha, he’s sitting there across from us, so offended that I didn’t ask him to sit before you. Ugh, Rakitin, you’re such a one for taking offense!” laughed Grushenka. “Don’t be angry, Rakitin, I’m kind today. Why are you so gloomy, Alyosha? Are you afraid of me?” She peered into his eyes with merry mockery.
“He’s sad. The promotion hasn’t come through,” boomed Rakitin.
“What promotion?”
“His elder stinks.”

“What? That’s nonsense, you just want to say something nasty. Shut up, you fool! Let me sit on your knee, Alyosha, like this.” She suddenly skipped forward and hopped onto his knee, laughing, like a kitten, with her right arm around his neck. “I’ll cheer you up, my pious boy. Really, will you let me sit here? You won’t be angry? Tell me, and I’ll get off.”

Alyosha said nothing. He sat there afraid to move. He heard her words, “Tell me, and I’ll get off,” but he did not answer. Still, nothing stirred in his heart of what Rakitin, say, watching him spitefully from his corner, might have expected or imagined. His great grief swallowed every feeling that might have been roused. If he had been able to think clearly just then, he would have seen that he was wearing the strongest armor against every lust and temptation. Yet, dazed as he was and crushed by sorrow, he could not help noticing a new and strange feeling in his heart. This woman, this “dreadful” woman, did not frighten him now. He felt none of the fear that used to rise in his soul whenever a thought of any woman crossed his mind. Quite the opposite. This was the woman he had feared more than any other, and she was sitting on his knee with her arms around him. She woke in him a different, unexpected, odd feeling: the keenest, purest interest, with no trace of his old terror. That was what instinctively surprised him.
“You’ve talked enough nonsense,” cried Rakitin. “You’d be better off giving us some champagne. You owe it to me, and you know it!”

“Yes, I do. Do you know, Alyosha, on top of everything else I promised him champagne if he’d bring you here? I’ll have some too! Fenya, Fenya, bring the bottle Mitya left! Be quick! I’m stingy, but I’ll stand you a bottle anyway. Not for you, Rakitin, you’re a toadstool, but he’s a falcon! My heart is full of something very different, but never mind, I’ll drink with you. I feel like letting myself go.”
“But what’s wrong with you? And what is this message, if I may ask? Or is it a secret?” Rakitin put in, curious, doing his best to look as if he hadn’t noticed the snubs that kept coming his way.

“Ech, it’s no secret, and you know it,” Grushenka said, her voice suddenly anxious. She turned toward Rakitin and drew a little away from Alyosha, though she still sat on his knee with her arm around his neck. “My officer is coming, Rakitin. My officer is coming.”
“I heard he was coming, but is he that close already?”
“He’s at Mokroe now. He’ll send a messenger from there, he wrote. I got his letter today. I’m expecting the messenger any minute.”
“You don’t say! Why Mokroe?”
“That’s a long story. I’ve told you enough.”
“Mitya will be up to something now! Tell me, does he know or doesn’t he?”

“Does he know! Of course not. If he knew, there’d be murder. But I’m not afraid of that now, I’m not afraid of his knife. Quiet, Rakitin, don’t remind me of Dmitri Fyodorovitch. He’s bruised my heart. I don’t want to think about that right now. I can think about Alyosha, I can look at Alyosha ... smile at me, dear, cheer up, smile at my silliness, at my happiness.... Ah, he’s smiling, he’s smiling! How kindly he looks at me! And you know, Alyosha, all this time I’ve been thinking you were angry with me about the day before yesterday, about that young lady. I behaved like a cur, that’s the truth.... But it’s good that it happened. It was horrid, but good as well.” Grushenka smiled dreamily, and a faintly cruel line showed in her smile. “Mitya told me she screamed that I ‘ought to be flogged.’ I did insult her terribly. She sent for me, she wanted to make a conquest of me, to win me over with her chocolate.... No, it’s good that it ended like that.” She smiled again. “But I’m still afraid you’re angry with me.”
“Well, that’s really true,” Rakitin put in suddenly, genuinely surprised. “Alyosha, she’s honestly afraid of a chicken like you.”
“He’s a chicken to you, Rakitin ... because you have no conscience, that’s why! You see, I love him with my whole soul, that’s how it is! Alyosha, do you believe I love you with my whole soul?”
“Ah, you shameless woman! She’s declaring herself to you, Alexey!”
“So what? I love him!”
“And your officer? And the priceless message from Mokroe?”
“That’s something else entirely.”
“That’s a woman’s way of looking at it!”

“Don’t make me angry, Rakitin.” Grushenka cut in hotly. “It’s something else entirely. I love Alyosha in another way. It’s true, Alyosha, I had sly plans for you once. I’m a horrid, violent creature. But at other times I’ve looked at you, Alyosha, as my conscience. I kept thinking, ‘How someone like him must despise a nasty thing like me.’ I thought that the day before yesterday, running home from the young lady’s. I’ve thought of you this way for a long time, Alyosha, and Mitya knows, I’ve talked to him about it. Mitya understands. Believe it or not, there are times I look at you and feel ashamed, completely ashamed of myself.... How and since when I started thinking of you like this, I can’t say, I don’t remember....”
Fenya came in and set a tray on the table, with an open bottle and three glasses of champagne.

“The champagne!” cried Rakitin. “You’re worked up, Agrafena Alexandrovna, you’re not yourself. One glass of champagne and you’ll be ready to dance. Eh, they can’t even manage this properly,” he added, looking at the bottle. “The old woman poured it in the kitchen, and the bottle’s come in warm, with no cork. Well, give me some anyway.”
He went to the table, took a glass, drank it off in one gulp and poured himself another.

“You don’t often come across champagne,” he said, licking his lips. “Now, Alyosha, take a glass, show us what you’re made of! What shall we drink to? The gates of paradise? Take a glass, Grushenka, you drink to the gates of paradise too.”
“What gates of paradise?”
She took a glass. Alyosha took his, sipped it and put it down.
“No, I’d rather not,” he said with a gentle smile.
“And you bragged!” cried Rakitin.
“Then I won’t either,” chimed in Grushenka. “I don’t really want any. You can drink the whole bottle alone, Rakitin. If Alyosha drinks, I will.”

“How touching and sentimental!” said Rakitin with a sneer. “And she’s sitting on his knee, too! He has something to grieve over, but what’s the matter with you? He’s rebelling against his God and ready to eat sausage....”
“What do you mean?”
“His elder died today. Father Zossima, the saint.”

“So Father Zossima is dead,” cried Grushenka. “Good God, I didn’t know!” She crossed herself devoutly. “Heavens, what am I doing, sitting on his knee like this at a time like this!” She jumped up as if in alarm, slipped off his knee at once and sat down on the sofa.
Alyosha looked at her for a long time, wondering, and a light seemed to dawn on his face.

“Rakitin,” he said suddenly, in a firm, loud voice, “don’t taunt me that I’ve rebelled against God. I don’t want to be angry with you, so be kinder yourself. I’ve lost a treasure that you’ve never had, and you can’t judge me now. Look at her instead. Do you see how she pities me? I came here looking for a wicked soul. I was drawn to evil because I was base and evil myself. And I’ve found a true sister, I’ve found a treasure, a loving heart. She pitied me just now.... Agrafena Alexandrovna, I’m speaking of you. You’ve lifted my soul out of the depths.”
Alyosha’s lips were trembling, and he was catching his breath.
“So she’s saved you, it seems,” laughed Rakitin spitefully. “And she meant to get you in her clutches, you know that?”

“Wait, Rakitin.” Grushenka sprang up. “Quiet, both of you. Now I’ll tell you everything. Quiet, Alyosha, your words shame me, because I’m bad, not good. That’s what I am. And you be quiet, Rakitin, because you’re lying. It’s true that I had the low idea of getting him into my clutches, but now you’re lying, now everything is different. I don’t want to hear another word from you, Rakitin.”
Grushenka said all this in great agitation.
“They’re both crazy,” said Rakitin, staring at them in amazement. “I feel like I’m in a madhouse. They’re both going so soft that they’ll start crying in a minute.”
“I will cry, I will,” repeated Grushenka. “He called me his sister, and I’ll never forget it. But let me tell you, Rakitin, bad as I am, I did give away an onion.”
“An onion? Damn it, you really are crazy.”

Rakitin was amazed at their heat. He was hurt and annoyed, though he might have considered that each of them was passing through a crisis of the soul, the kind that doesn’t come often in a lifetime. But Rakitin was touchy about anything that concerned himself and very thick-skinned about what other people felt. That came partly from his youth and inexperience, and partly from his enormous egoism.

“You see, Alyosha,” Grushenka said, turning to him with a nervous laugh, “I was bragging when I told Rakitin I’d given away an onion. I’m not telling you to brag. It’s just a story, but it’s a nice one. I heard it as a child from Matryona, my cook, who still works for me. It goes like this. Once there was a peasant woman, and a very wicked woman she was. She died without leaving a single good deed behind her. The devils seized her and threw her into the lake of fire. Her guardian angel stood by, wondering what good deed of hers he could remember to tell God. ‘She pulled up an onion once in her garden,’ he said, ‘and gave it to a beggar woman.’ And God answered: ‘Take that onion, then, and hold it out to her in the lake. Let her take hold and be pulled out. If you can pull her out of the lake, she may come to Paradise. But if the onion breaks, she must stay where she is.’ The angel ran to the woman and held the onion out to her. ‘Here,’ he said, ‘take hold, and I’ll pull you out.’ And he began pulling her out, carefully. He had just got her all the way out when the other sinners in the lake saw her being pulled up, and began grabbing at her to be pulled out too. But she was a very wicked woman, and she began kicking them. ‘I’m the one being pulled out, not you. It’s my onion, not yours.’ The moment she said it, the onion broke. The woman fell back into the lake, and she’s burning there to this day. So the angel wept and went away. That’s the story, Alyosha. I know it by heart, because I’m that wicked woman myself. I bragged to Rakitin that I’d given away an onion, but to you I’ll say: ‘All my life I’ve done nothing but give away one onion, that’s the only good deed I’ve ever done.’ So don’t praise me, Alyosha, don’t think I’m good. I’m bad, I’m a wicked woman, and you make me ashamed if you praise me. Eh, I have to confess everything. Listen, Alyosha. I wanted so badly to get hold of you that I promised Rakitin twenty-five roubles if he’d bring you to me. Wait, Rakitin, stay where you are!”
She went briskly to the table, opened a drawer, took out a purse and drew a twenty-five rouble note from it.
“What nonsense! What nonsense!” cried Rakitin, thrown off balance.
“Take it. I owe it to you, Rakitin. I know you won’t refuse it, you asked for it yourself.” And she tossed the note to him.
“As if I’d refuse,” boomed Rakitin, plainly embarrassed but covering it with a swagger. “It will come in very handy. Fools exist for the profit of wise men.”
“And now keep your mouth shut, Rakitin. What I’m going to say is not for your ears. Sit in that corner and be quiet. You don’t like us, so hold your tongue.”

“Why would I like you?” Rakitin snarled, making no effort to hide his bad temper. He put the twenty-five rouble note in his pocket, ashamed that Alyosha had seen it. He had counted on being paid later, without Alyosha knowing, and now, feeling ashamed, he lost his temper. Until then he had thought it wise not to contradict Grushenka too bluntly, despite her snubs, since he wanted something out of her. But now he was angry too.
“You love people for a reason. But what have either of you ever done for me?”
“You should love people for no reason, the way Alyosha does.”
“How does he love you? What has he done to show it, that you make such a fuss?”
Grushenka stood in the middle of the room. She spoke heatedly, and her voice had a hysterical edge.

“Be quiet, Rakitin, you know nothing about us! And don’t you dare talk to me like that again. How dare you be so familiar! Sit in that corner and keep quiet, as if you were my footman! And now, Alyosha, I’ll tell you the whole truth, so you can see what a wretch I am! I’m not talking to Rakitin, I’m talking to you. I wanted to ruin you, Alyosha, that’s the holy truth. I was fully set on it. I wanted it so badly that I bribed Rakitin to bring you. And why did I want to do such a thing? You knew nothing about it, Alyosha. You turned away from me, and when you passed me you lowered your eyes. I’d looked at you a hundred times before today. I started asking everybody about you. Your face haunted my heart. ‘He despises me,’ I thought, ‘he won’t even look at me.’ In the end it hurt so much that I was amazed at myself, being so afraid of a boy. I’ll get him in my clutches and laugh at him, I thought. I was full of spite and anger. Believe me, nobody here dares to speak, or even think, of coming to Agrafena Alexandrovna with any bad intention. Old Kuzma is the only man I have anything to do with here. I was bound and sold to him. Satan brought us together, but there’s been no one else. But looking at you, I thought, I’ll get him in my clutches and laugh at him. You see what a spiteful cur I am, and you called me your sister! And now the man who wronged me has come. I’m sitting here waiting for word from him. And do you know what that man has been to me? Five years ago, when Kuzma brought me here, I used to lock myself in so nobody could see or hear me. I was a silly slip of a girl. I used to sit here sobbing. I used to lie awake all night thinking: ‘Where is he now, the man who wronged me? He’s laughing at me with some other woman, I bet. If only I could see him, if I could meet him again, I’d pay him back, I’d pay him back!’ At night I’d lie in the dark sobbing into my pillow, brooding over it. I used to tear at my own heart on purpose and gloat over my anger. ‘I’ll pay him back, I’ll pay him back!’ That’s what I’d cry out in the dark. And when I suddenly thought that really I would do nothing to him, and that he was laughing at me then, or maybe had forgotten me completely, I’d throw myself on the floor, break down in helpless tears, and lie there shaking until dawn. In the morning I’d get up meaner than a dog, ready to tear the whole world to pieces. And then what do you think? I started saving money, I grew hard-hearted, I got stout. Wiser, would you say? No, nobody in the whole world sees it, nobody knows it. But when night comes, I sometimes lie just as I did five years ago, when I was a silly girl, clenching my teeth and crying all night, thinking, ‘I’ll pay him back, I’ll pay him back!’ Do you hear? Well, now you understand me. A month ago a letter came. He was coming, he was a widower, he wanted to see me. It took my breath away. Then I suddenly thought: ‘If he comes and whistles for me, I’ll crawl back to him like a beaten dog.’ I couldn’t believe it of myself. Am I really so low? Will I run to him or not? I’ve been in such a rage with myself all this month that I’m worse than I was five years ago. Do you see now, Alyosha, what a violent, vengeful creature I am? I’ve told you the whole truth! I played with Mitya to keep myself from running to that other man. Quiet, Rakitin, it’s not for you to judge me, I’m not speaking to you. Before you came in, I was lying here waiting, brooding, deciding my whole life to come, and you can never know what was in my heart. Yes, Alyosha, tell your young lady not to be angry with me for what happened the day before yesterday.... Nobody in the whole world knows what I’m going through now, and nobody ever can know.... Because maybe I’ll take a knife with me today, I can’t make up my mind ...”
And at that “tragic” phrase Grushenka broke down. She hid her face in her hands, threw herself onto the sofa cushions and sobbed like a little child.
Alyosha got up and went over to Rakitin.
“Misha,” he said, “don’t be angry. She hurt you, but don’t be angry. Did you hear what she just said? You mustn’t ask too much of human endurance. One has to be merciful.”

Alyosha said this because his heart prompted him to, without stopping to think. He felt he had to speak, and he turned to Rakitin. If Rakitin hadn’t been there, he would have spoken to the empty air. But Rakitin gave him a mocking look, and Alyosha broke off.
“You were stuffed so full of your elder’s teaching last night that now you have to unload it on me, Alexey, man of God!” said Rakitin, with a hateful smile.

“Don’t laugh, Rakitin, don’t smile, and don’t talk about the dead. He was better than anyone in the world!” cried Alyosha, with tears in his voice. “I wasn’t speaking to you as a judge, but as the lowest of the judged. What am I next to her? I came here looking for my own ruin, and I told myself, ‘What does it matter?’ out of cowardice. But she has suffered for five years, and the moment anyone says a word to her from the heart, she forgets everything and forgives everything, in her tears! The man who wronged her has come back and sent for her, and she forgives him everything and hurries joyfully to meet him, and she won’t take a knife with her. She won’t! No, I am not like that. I don’t know whether you are, Misha, but I am not like that. It’s a lesson to me.... She has more love in her than we have.... Have you ever heard her say before what she has just told us? No, you haven’t. If you had, you’d have understood her long ago ... and the person who was insulted the day before yesterday must forgive her, too! She will, once she knows ... and she shall know.... This soul isn’t yet at peace with itself. One must be tender with it ... there may be a treasure in that soul....”
Alyosha stopped, because he had run out of breath. Bad mood or not, Rakitin stared at him in astonishment. He had never expected a speech like that from gentle Alyosha.
“She’s found someone to plead her case! What, are you in love with her? Agrafena Alexandrovna, our monk is really in love with you. You’ve made a conquest!” he cried, with a coarse laugh.
Grushenka lifted her head from the pillow. Her face was wet with tears, and a tender smile shone through them as she looked at Alyosha.

“Leave him be, Alyosha, my cherub. You can see what he is. He’s no one for you to talk to. Mihail Osipovitch,” she turned to Rakitin, “I was going to apologize for being rude to you, but now I won’t. Alyosha, come here and sit by me.” She beckoned him with a happy smile. “Yes, like that, sit here. Tell me,” she shook him by the hand and peered into his face, smiling, “tell me, do I love that man or don’t I? The one who wronged me, do I love him? Before you came I was lying here in the dark, asking my heart that very question. You decide for me, Alyosha. The time has come, and whatever you say is how it will be. Do I forgive him, or not?”
“But you have forgiven him already,” said Alyosha, smiling.

“Yes, I have forgiven him, really,” Grushenka murmured thoughtfully. “What a wretched heart I have! Here’s to my wretched heart!” She snatched up a glass from the table, drained it in one gulp, held it high and hurled it to the floor. It smashed with a crash. A small, cruel line crept into her smile.

“Perhaps I haven’t forgiven him, though,” she said, with a kind of menace in her voice, her eyes dropping to the floor as if she were talking to herself. “Perhaps my heart is only getting ready to forgive. I’ll fight with my heart. You see, Alyosha, in these five years I’ve grown to love my tears.... Perhaps it’s only my resentment I love, not him ...”
“Well, I wouldn’t care to be in his shoes,” Rakitin hissed.
“Well, you won’t be, Rakitin. You’ll never be in his shoes. You shall black my shoes, Rakitin. That’s where you belong. You’ll never get a woman like me ... and he won’t either, perhaps ...”
“Won’t he? Then why are you dressed up like that?” said Rakitin, with a venomous sneer.

“Don’t taunt me about dressing up, Rakitin. You don’t know everything that’s in my heart! If I choose to tear off my finery, I’ll tear it off at once, this minute,” she cried in a ringing voice. “You don’t know what that finery is for, Rakitin! Perhaps I’ll see him and say, ‘Have you ever seen me look like this before?’ He left me a thin, consumptive crybaby of seventeen. I’ll sit beside him, fascinate him and work him up. ‘Do you see what I’m like now?’ I’ll say to him. ‘Well, that’s all you’re getting, my dear sir. There’s many a slip between the cup and the lip!’ That may be what the finery is for, Rakitin.” Grushenka finished with a spiteful laugh. “I’m violent and I hold grudges, Alyosha. I’ll tear off my finery, I’ll destroy my beauty, I’ll scorch my face, slash it with a knife, and turn beggar. If I choose, I won’t go anywhere now to see anyone. If I choose, I’ll send Kuzma back everything he has ever given me, tomorrow, and all his money, and I’ll go out scrubbing floors for the rest of my life. You think I wouldn’t do it, Rakitin? That I wouldn’t dare? I would, I would, I could do it right now, only don’t push me ... and I’ll send him about his business, I’ll snap my fingers in his face, and he’ll never see me again!”
She screamed the last words hysterically, then broke down again, hid her face in her hands, buried it in the pillow and shook with sobs.
Rakitin got up.
“It’s time we left,” he said. “It’s late, and we’ll be locked out of the monastery.”
Grushenka sprang up from where she sat.

“You can’t mean you’re leaving, Alyosha!” she cried, sad and amazed. “What have you done to me? You’ve stirred up all my feelings and tortured me, and now you’re going to leave me alone with this night!”
“Well, he can’t very well stay the night with you! Although if he wants to, let him! I’ll go by myself,” Rakitin jeered.
“Quiet, you evil tongue!” Grushenka cried angrily at him. “You never said to me the words he came to say.”
“What did he say to you that was so special?” asked Rakitin irritably.

“I can’t say, I don’t know. I don’t know what he said to me, only that it went straight to my heart. He has wrung my heart out.... He is the first, the only one, who has pitied me, that’s all it is. Why didn’t you come sooner, you angel?” She dropped to her knees before him as if in a sudden fit of frenzy. “All my life I’ve been waiting for someone like you. I knew someone like you would come and forgive me. I believed that, nasty as I am, someone would truly love me, and not just with a shameful love!”
“What have I done to you?” Alyosha answered. He bent over her with a tender smile and took her gently by the hands. “I gave you an onion, that’s all, one tiny little onion!”

He was moved to tears himself as he said it. Just then there was a sudden noise in the passage, and someone came into the hall. Grushenka jumped to her feet, looking badly frightened. Fenya came running noisily into the room, crying out:

“Mistress, mistress darling, a messenger has galloped up,” she cried, out of breath and joyful. “There’s a carriage from Mokroe for you, with Timofey the driver and three horses. They’re just changing the horses.... A letter, here’s the letter, mistress.”
She held a letter and waved it in the air the whole time she was talking. Grushenka snatched it from her and took it to the candle. It was only a note, a few lines long. She read it in a moment.
“He’s sent for me,” she cried, her face white and twisted, a pale smile on her lips. “He whistles! Crawl back, little dog!”
But she stood there hesitating for only a moment. Then the blood suddenly rushed to her head and set her cheeks glowing.

“I’m going,” she cried. “Five years of my life! Good-by! Good-by, Alyosha, my fate is decided. Go, all of you, go away, don’t let me see you again! Grushenka is flying off to a new life.... And don’t you keep anything against me either, Rakitin. I may be going to my death! Ugh! I feel as if I were drunk!”
She suddenly left them and ran into her bedroom.
“Well, she hasn’t a thought to spare for us now!” grumbled Rakitin. “Come on, before we hear that female screeching again. I’m sick to death of all these tears and cries.”

Alyosha let himself be led out like a man walking in his sleep. A covered cart stood in the yard. The horses were being unhitched from the shafts, and men ran back and forth with a lantern. Three fresh horses were being led in through the open gate. But as Alyosha and Rakitin reached the foot of the steps, Grushenka’s bedroom window suddenly flew open, and she called out after Alyosha in a ringing voice:

“Alyosha, give my greetings to your brother Mitya, and tell him not to hold it against me, even though I’ve brought him misery. And tell him this too, in my own words: ‘Grushenka has gone to a scoundrel, and not to you, noble heart.’ And add that Grushenka loved him for one hour only, one short hour she loved him—so let him remember that hour all his life—say, ‘Grushenka tells you to!’”
She ended in a voice full of sobs. The window shut with a slam.
“H’m, h’m!” growled Rakitin with a laugh. “She murders your brother Mitya, and then orders him to remember it all his life! What savagery!”

Alyosha made no reply. He seemed not to have heard. He walked fast beside Rakitin as if in a terrible hurry, lost in thought and moving like a man in a trance. Rakitin felt a sudden twinge, as if someone had touched an open wound. He had expected something quite different from bringing Grushenka and Alyosha together. What had happened was nothing like what he had hoped for.

“He’s a Pole, that officer of hers,” he began again, holding himself in. “And really he’s not an officer at all now. He served in the customs in Siberia, somewhere on the Chinese frontier, some puny little beggar of a Pole, I expect. Lost his job, they say. Now he’s heard that Grushenka has saved a little money, so he’s turned up again. That’s the explanation of the mystery.”
Again Alyosha seemed not to hear. Rakitin couldn’t control himself.

“Well, so you’ve saved the sinner?” he laughed spitefully. “Put the Magdalene on the straight path? Cast out the seven devils, eh? So the miracles you were hoping for a while ago have come true after all!”
“Hush, Rakitin,” Alyosha answered, with an aching heart.
“So you despise me now for those twenty-five roubles? You think I’ve sold my friend. But you’re not Christ, you know, and I’m not Judas.”
“Oh, Rakitin, I assure you I’d forgotten about it,” cried Alyosha. “You’re the one reminding me of it....”
But this was the last straw for Rakitin.
“Damn the lot of you!” he cried suddenly. “Why the devil did I ever take you up? From now on I don’t want to know you. Go on alone, there’s your road!”
And he turned sharply down another street and left Alyosha alone in the dark. Alyosha left the town and crossed the fields toward the monastery.
